**Q1: In your own words, what was the main reason you didn't come back after the first meeting?**

- **Respondent 1:** "The room felt a bit cliquey, and I didn't feel I could just join in with anyone."
- **Respondent 2:** "I didn't follow much of the discussion, and I wasn't sure I was supposed to understand it all."
- **Respondent 3:** "I'm already committed to several other groups, and I didn't see what this one would add."
- **Respondent 4:** "The meeting time clashed with my work shifts, so I couldn't make it back."
- **Respondent 5:** "A couple of members dominated the discussion, and it didn't feel like my views were wanted."
- **Respondent 6:** "I got bored in the meeting and didn't see a reason to go back."
- **Respondent 7:** "I was told the club is for people who already know the subject, and I wasn't sure I qualified."
- **Respondent 8:** "I had a bad experience with a member who pressured me to buy merchandise, and I've been avoiding the club since."

**Q3: If the club could change just one thing, what should it be?**

- **Respondent 1:** "Have someone actively invite newcomers to sit with them and introduce them to the group."
- **Respondent 2:** "Explain the terms and what the club is working towards at the start of each meeting."
- **Respondent 3:** "Be clearer about what the club offers that other groups don't, or work more closely with them."
- **Respondent 4:** "Hold meetings at a time that works for people who work evenings or shifts."
- **Respondent 5:** "Share out the discussion so quieter members get a turn and feel their input counts."
- **Respondent 6:** "Keep the talks and discussions as the core of the club, and make them more engaging rather than adding hands-on activities."
- **Respondent 7:** "Make it clear that beginners are welcome, and offer some introductory material for newcomers."
- **Respondent 8:** "Make sure nobody is pressured to buy anything, and deal properly with members who do."

**Q3: What would the club have to do in the first ten minutes for you to come back?**

Respondent 1: "If someone who's already in the group came over and asked me to sit with them before things started, I'd probably stay."

Respondent 2: "Explain the terms in plain English at the start. I didn't want to keep asking what things meant, and I assumed I was the only one lost."

Respondent 3: "Tell me in the first ten minutes what this club offers that I can't get from the group I already do. If it doesn't, I won't have time to come back."

Respondent 4: "Hold it at a time I can get to after my shifts. I can't keep missing it, and I'd make it if it fit."

Respondent 5: "Make sure everyone gets a turn before the discussion settles. Otherwise the same two people end up running it and the rest of us stop bothering."

Respondent 6: "Tell me up front that it stays a discussion club and isn't going to turn into hands-on activities. If the talk stays the focus, I'd give it another go."

Respondent 7: "Open with a short beginners' intro that says plainly that the club is for people who are new to the subject too. Then I'd know I belong and would come back."

Respondent 8: "Say at the start that nothing is for sale and nobody will push you to buy or join anything. Without that I'm not going to feel comfortable coming back."

steps.recommendation: Make the first ten minutes newcomer-friendly. Open every meeting with a short plain-language beginners' intro that says newcomers are welcome and explains the terms. Pair that with a named person who greets newcomers and sits with them. Intro and greeter tied on average rank, but the intro got the most first places. Also say plainly that nothing is for sale. Changing the meeting time or adding hands-on activities ranked low.
steps.evidence: Both rounds had 8 of 8 respondents. Round 1 ranking (avg rank, lower is better): clearer plan 2.25, welcome 2.38 (4 first places), cost 3.13, time 3.38, shorter meeting 3.88, hands-on 6.0 (0 first places). Round 1 reasons were all different: cliquey or dominated discussion (2), lost or unsure beginners were welcome (2), schedule clash (1), already in other groups (1), bored (1), pressured to buy merchandise (1). Round 2 ranking: beginners' intro 2.13 (3 first places), greeter 2.13 (1), clear offer 2.63 (2), everyone gets a turn 3.75, shift-friendly time 4.38. Round 2 pressure to buy or join: Yes 1, No 7.

steps.learned_between_rounds: Round 1 showed scattered reasons and two top options, welcome and clarity, that were close together. I used round 2 to separate them, and they tied again on average rank. It also checked how widespread the merchandise pressure was: 1 of 8.
steps.limits: Only 8 people, so this is a direction and not a measurement. The tie between intro and greeter was not resolved. The pressure-to-buy report comes from one person. Every Flashpoint reply was labelled as a practice stand-in, so the results may be simulated. I did not run a persona rehearsal.
lessons: Open-ended reasons from a small group scatter. Ranking plus 'what would bring you back' gave the usable signal.
Two top options tied again when re-ranked. A different design, such as a forced trade-off, may be needed to split them.
Ask openly about uncomfortable incidents. One surprise (pressure to buy) only came up because of the open question.
